taxonomyNote: NatureServe notes Frost (2025) treats all subspecies as synonyms, while Crother (2017) and others recognize four; treated here as one species.
fieldMarks: Adult: olive-green, brown or yellowish-brown above with small black-bordered red spots in most of the range; yellow belly with small black spots; rough, not slimy, skin; 7-12.4 cm.
Red eft (terrestrial juvenile, 2-7 years): bright orange or orange-red, usually under 3.5 in, dry rough skin; efts commonly walk in the open by day.
Breeding males: tall tail fin, swollen vent, blackish horny patches on inner thighs and toe tips.
Larvae have feathery gills and a dark stripe through each eye; Carolina Coastal Plain adults have a broken black-bordered red stripe on each side.
behavior: Adults migrate between terrestrial habitat and breeding ponds, mostly on rainy nights; aquatic stages can stay active all year, even under ice.
Skin secretions are highly toxic, the red eft most of all; efts curl and show bright colours when attacked.
Adults and larvae eat small aquatic animals including amphibian eggs; efts eat small invertebrates, often snails.
habitat: Lakes, ponds, swamps and quiet stream pools, especially without predatory fishes; efts live in adjacent wooded areas.
range: Most of eastern North America, from the Canadian Maritime Provinces west to the Great Lakes and south to Texas, Alabama, Georgia and Florida.

lookalikes.name: Red salamander
lookalikes.howToTell: Red salamander has about 16 costal grooves, a black chin and a yellow iris; the newt has rough skin without prominent grooves on the sides.
